This paper finds that LLM agents chasing economic targets break financial rules on their own, even when they refuse direct requests to break them.

Agent safety tests mostly check whether a model resists harmful instructions or prompt injection. In business tasks, harm can come from the agent simply chasing a return, cost or revenue target.

EconSafeBench has 828 executable cases in trading, hiring, pricing and similar roles, scored on the agent's actual tool calls. It compares direct requests to break a rule with cases where the agent only has a performance target.

Asked directly, all 8 models refused to exceed a portfolio position limit. Given only a return target, 2 models broke it 92% and 94% of the time.

Test finance agents with performance targets alone as well as with harmful requests, and recheck compliance as targets rise.

New Google and Penn State paper finds that when one AI rewrites the code that gives another AI its instructions and tools, keeping notes on why each change was made helps the gains carry over to a new model.

LLMs can now rewrite an agent's harness, the code that runs prompts and tools. After a model or benchmark switch, it can score below the original, and its code hides why edits were made.

Self-Improvement Memory, or SIM, logs each edit with the problem it targeted, its reasoning and its measured result. The optimizer reads this log on the new setup to decide which old edits to keep or revise.

When a Claude Opus 5.5 harness moved to Gemini 3.8 Flash workspace tasks, SIM lifted it from 68.41 to 84.75, versus 73.42 without the log. Across 10 repeated coding runs, SIM finished ahead 9 times, by 2.36 points on average.

Store why each harness edit was made and how it scored, and carry that log to new models.

article.plain_text:
Sciforium’s latest DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash build reaches 1,129 output tokens per second at P90 on four AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, thanks to our traffic-tuned drafters. And no, we didn’t rewrite vLLM or SGLang from scratch in Rust! Here’s how we did it.
Building on our earlier megakernel work, we trained a traffic-tuned drafter to increase how many drafted tokens the main model accepts given a specific data distribution in the traffic, then extended the drafts from five tokens to seven after resolving stability issues. We combined this with Sciforium and AMD kernel optimizations, including our work to fuse intermediate operations and communication. Better drafts let each verification pass advance the response further, while the kernel work improved execution efficiency, turning the engineering improvements into faster output for the user. Before getting more into details, let me cover what speculative decoding is (for those 1% who still don't know) and then I will cover what a traffic-tuned drafter means in this context.
How speculative decoding works
Ordinary autoregressive generation produces one token at a time, with each token depending on the text before it. Speculative decoding uses a cheaper drafter to propose several upcoming tokens, which the main model checks together in a verification pass. The system keeps the accepted beginning of the proposal, corrects it where necessary, and continues. When several proposed tokens are accepted, one verification pass advances the response by several tokens. The drafter’s usefulness therefore depends on how much of its proposal survives that check.
 

Why acceptance length matters
Draft length is how many tokens we propose. Acceptance length describes how much of that proposal we can keep. Consider a five-token draft: if only the first two tokens are accepted, the rest of the proposal does not advance the response. If the first four are accepted, the verification round gets further. A better drafter makes longer accepted sequences more likely, allowing the system to obtain more useful output from each pass through the main model.
This distinction explains why increasing draft length alone can disappoint. If the main model rejects a proposal near the beginning, proposing more tokens beyond that point adds work without adding accepted output. Improving the drafter changes that tradeoff. Once proposals are accepted further into the sequence, longer drafts give the system more room to benefit from those better predictions. That was the motivation for testing seven-token drafts after improving acceptance with our traffic-tuned drafter.
 

How better acceptance translates into faster responses
For the user, what matters is how quickly the complete system produces output. Longer accepted sequences can reduce the number of verification rounds needed to generate a response, spreading the cost of those rounds across more tokens. But generating and checking longer proposals also takes time. Especially, when we increase the draft length, the verification process also becomes more expensive. So, the speedup depends on gaining enough useful output to outweigh that extra cost. Acceptance length helps explain why a configuration might be faster; measuring output tokens per second establishes whether it actually is. This improvement concerns the generation phase of a response, after output begins.
What we changed
We first trained a traffic-tuned drafter on the customer’s own traffic. We asked our existing customers to let us use their traffic to understand what their data looks like and how we can predict the majority of the expected responses in the speculative drafter instead of the main model. The drafters are tailored to their workload and exclusive to each customer.
With improved acceptance, we increased the proposal length from five tokens to seven. The extra two positions created an opportunity to accept more output in each round. Making that configuration usable required stability fixes for seven-token drafting, and the final benchmark includes those fixes. The decision was ultimately a performance tradeoff: the longer proposal had to produce enough additional accepted output to justify its drafting and verification cost.
We also optimized the operations surrounding the model’s major GPU kernels. Intermediate operations, including mHC and projections, offered opportunities for further fusion. We combined operations into fewer kernels and fused all-reduce communication with computation; all-reduce combines the partial results produced across the GPUs. This work targets the overhead of intermediate processing and data movement. Graph execution already removes the gaps between launches, so the benefit should not be understood as simply filling time when the GPUs would otherwise sit idle.
 
The execution strategy also changes with concurrency. Beyond eight concurrent requests, the existing megakernel approach showed diminishing returns, motivating further work on intermediate operations around the major kernels. We also tested running all-reduce on a separate execution stream to overlap communication with other work. That experiment did not help: the overlapping operations competed for memory bandwidth. Fusing computation and communication and scheduling separate operations simultaneously are different approaches, and the latter did not deliver a benefit in this test. This is why we evaluated the execution changes under their relevant load conditions rather than assuming every optimization would help equally at every concurrency.
Bringing the pieces together
The configuration that reached 1,129 output tokens per second combined DeepSeek’s original model weights, Sciforium and AMD kernel optimizations, the traffic-tuned drafter, and seven-token speculative drafts with the stability fixes in place. The result was measured on four MI355X GPUs using a long-context agentic workload. It represents the performance of that complete configuration; the separate kernel experiments at higher concurrency are not percentages to add onto the headline result.
 
At 1,129 output tokens per second, generating 10,000 tokens takes roughly nine seconds, excluding prompt processing and tool execution. We achieved this rate at P90 on four AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs while retaining DeepSeek’s original main-model weights. The gains came from improving how we serve the model: better draft predictions, more accepted tokens per verification pass, and more efficient GPU execution.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a model serving production traffic on AMD GPUs has exceeded 1,000 output tokens per second. It’s a milestone in our work to turn AMD’s hardware capabilities into production performance, and we’ll keep pushing for faster, more efficient inference.
